catalog_quote: Each Chorei content word has one primary stress. The existence of stress in Chorei is confirmed by its effects on the word-structure, e.g. pre-tonic vowel deletion (§2.4.2) and shortening of vowels in unstressed open syllables (§2.4.4), which are both typical of stress systems (Kager 2007, 195, 198). The primary stress in Chorei words lies on the last syllable of the lexeme. Usually, this is the root of the word, as the commonest Chorei derivational morphology is prefixal (§3.1). However, when a derivational suffix occurs, it receives the stress, e.g. dông-mâ /dɔːŋˈmaː/ ‘family-FEM > wife’. In contrast, inflectional suffixes, e.g. -â /aː/ ‘LOC’, are normally unstressed, e.g. ray-â /ˈra.jaː/ ‘axe-LOC > on the axe’. Prefixes, whether derivational or inflectional, are never stressed. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (lexeme) stress is fixed on the final syllable of the lexical stem: the last root syllable, or a derivational suffix if one follows; prefixes (derivational or inflectional agreement proclitics) are never stressed and inflectional suffixes/enclitics (e.g. locative -â, plural -ngay, nominalizer -nâ) normally fall outside the stress domain, so in fully inflected words stress is stem-final rather than strictly word-final. Main acoustic correlate is intensity, secondarily duration. The language (as spoken by most speakers in Manikbond) has no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'The occurrence and characteristics of secondary stress in Chorei is currently not well-understood'; non-lexeme-final lexical roots in compounds (e.g. kê in kê-kadoy /(ˌ)keː.kaˈdɔj/, dông in dông-mâ) are possible bearers of secondary stress (they keep length contrast in closed syllables and can trigger vowel harmony), but this could not be confirmed, so all syllables without primary stress are treated as unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal negative suffixes -mak 'NFUT.NEG', -nô 'FUT.NEG', -loy '?.NEG' attract stress although expected to be inflectional (ni-ˈmak, sa-ˈloy, with shortening of the root vowel); nominalizer -nâ stays unstressed although derivational-like; grammaticalizing -(n)zay 'PFV' is variably stressed (a-ˈkang-zay vs a-hek-ˈzay); status of postposed grammatical words such as comparative naykin (separate phonological word vs. phrase-final intonational prominence) unresolved.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexeme/phonological word ('Each Chorei content word has one primary stress'); based mainly on a c. 1000-item wordlist elicited from four speakers plus limited connected speech, Manikbond village (Assam, near Tripura/Mizoram border), Feb-Apr 2025; author notes higher-level prosody is not yet analysed. NOTE the variety: this is Chorei (Glottolog dialect chor1278 of saka1283 'Sakachep-Chorei'), not Khelma/Sakachep proper, for which the two accessible phonologies (Borgohain & Khyriem 2022; Bhattacharyya & Dutta 2021 per editorial summary) report lexical tone (3 resp. 2 tones) and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes CHOREI (Glottolog dialect-level code chor1278, listed under saka1283 'Sakachep-Chorei', ISO sch), as spoken in Manikbond village, Assam (Tripura/Mizoram border), which its speakers and the author treat as a distinct but mutually intelligible variety alongside Sakachep/Khelma, Ranglong and Hrangkhol. For KHELMA/SAKACHEP proper (Dima Hasao, Barak Valley, Meghalaya; dialects Hanle and Hante per the 2017 learner's book) the accessible descriptions are tonal and silent on stress: Borgohain & Khyriem 2022 (NEHU) report three register tones (high/mid/low); Bhattacharyya & Dutta 2021 (Tezpur CFEL, not online) reportedly two lexical tones. Jana 2025 finds Chorei NON-tonal with lexeme-final stress, so the prosodic description may not transfer to Sakachep proper; a catalog entry should be labelled 'Chorei (chor1278)' or flagged as dialect-specific.

sources.note: Ch. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology', 4.1 Stress (p. 51-53): every content word has one primary stress, on the last syllable of the lexeme (usually the root; a derivational suffix if present takes it); inflectional suffixes normally unstressed, prefixes never stressed; main correlate intensity (+ some duration); evidence from pre-tonic vowel deletion and unstressed open-syllable vowel shortening; secondary stress on non-final roots possible but unconfirmed; negative suffixes -mak/-no/-loy attract stress. 4.2: tones absent for most speakers (one elderly speaker produced unverified pitch contrasts).
